topics.name: Stress, Strain, and Hooke's Law
topics.summary: Stress is the internal restoring force per unit area that a deformed body develops, \( \sigma = F/A \), measured in N/m\(^2\) (pascal). Strain is the fractional change in a dimension and has no unit: longitudinal strain is \( \Delta L/L \), shearing strain is the small angle \( \theta \) (in radians) through which a layer tilts, and volume strain is \( \Delta V/V \). Three kinds of stress go with them: tensile or compressive (force normal to the face), tangential or shearing (force parallel to the face), and hydraulic (uniform pressure on all sides). Hooke's law is the experimental fact that, for small deformations, stress is directly proportional to strain; the constant of proportionality is a modulus of elasticity and depends on the material and on the type of deformation. The law holds only in the initial straight-line region of the stress-strain graph. Poisson's ratio, \( \nu = -(\text{lateral strain})/(\text{longitudinal strain}) \), is a positive pure number that tells how much a stretched wire thins. Always convert mm and mm\(^2\) to SI before computing, and remember that a wire hanging under its own weight has the largest stress at its top.
topics.worked_example:
A wire of length 4 m and area 2 mm\(^2\) stretches by 2 mm under 400 N.

Area \( = 2\times10^{-6} \) m\(^2\), so stress \( = \dfrac{400}{2\times10^{-6}} = 2\times10^{8} \) Pa.

Strain \( = \dfrac{2\times10^{-3}}{4} = 5\times10^{-4} \), a pure number.
common_mistakes: Dividing force by length instead of area, or leaving the area in mm\(^2\)
Giving strain a unit, or inverting it as original length over extension
Treating stress as proportional to the square of strain, or assuming Hooke's law holds for every load
Using the diameter ratio instead of its square when comparing stresses in wires of different thickness

topics.name: Stress-Strain Curve: Elastic Limit, Yield Point, and Fracture
topics.summary: When a metal wire is loaded gradually and its stress is plotted against strain, four different points appear in a fixed order. Up to the proportional limit the graph is a straight line through the origin and Hooke's law holds. Slightly beyond it lies the elastic limit: the curve has begun to bend, but on unloading the wire still returns exactly to its original length. Beyond the elastic limit some deformation is permanent (plastic). At the yield point the material gives way, and strain increases greatly for almost no increase in stress; the stress there is the yield strength. The curve then rises to its highest point, the ultimate tensile strength, after which the wire necks and finally breaks at the fracture point. A ductile material has a long plastic region between elastic limit and fracture and can be drawn into wires; a brittle material fractures almost immediately after its elastic limit. Elastomers such as rubber have no straight-line region at all yet recover from very large strains. The slope of the initial line is Young's modulus, and Hooke's law is an empirical rule valid only for small strains.
key_formulas: Order along the curve: proportional limit, elastic limit, yield point, ultimate tensile strength, fracture point
Elastic strain recovered \( = \) total strain \( - \) permanent strain
Strain at a limiting stress (linear region) \( = \dfrac{\sigma_{limit}}{Y} \)
topics.worked_example:
A steel wire (\( Y = 2\times10^{11} \) Pa) reaches its elastic limit at a stress of \( 2\times10^{8} \) Pa.

Maximum recoverable strain \( = \dfrac{2\times10^{8}}{2\times10^{11}} = 10^{-3} \).

For a 2 m wire this is an extension of 2 mm; stretching it by 3 mm would leave a permanent set.
common_mistakes: Treating the proportional limit and the elastic limit as the same point
Believing Hooke's law holds all the way to the yield point or fracture point
Swapping the yield point and the fracture point, or thinking that exceeding the elastic limit means the wire breaks
Calling rubber inelastic because it does not obey Hooke's law

topics.name: Young's Modulus: Elongation, Compression, and Combined-Wire Problems
topics.summary: Young's modulus \( Y \) is the ratio of longitudinal stress to longitudinal strain, \( Y = \dfrac{FL}{A\,\Delta L} \), with unit N/m\(^2\). It is a property of the material alone: steel about \( 2\times10^{11} \) Pa, copper \( 1.1\times10^{11} \) Pa, aluminium \( 7\times10^{10} \) Pa. The larger \( Y \), the smaller the strain for a given stress, so in physics steel is more elastic than rubber. Rearranging gives the extension (or compression) \( \Delta L = \dfrac{FL}{AY} \): it grows with load and length and shrinks with area and modulus, so a wire behaves as a spring of constant \( k = \dfrac{YA}{L} \). Combined wires follow two different rules. Joined end to end (series), each wire carries the whole load, the stress is the same if the areas are equal, and the extensions add. Hung side by side and loaded through a rigid bar (parallel), the extensions are equal and the loads add, each wire taking a share proportional to its own \( \dfrac{YA}{L} \). Poisson's ratio links the lateral thinning to the longitudinal stretch: lateral strain \( = -\nu\,\varepsilon \). Always convert areas to m\(^2\) and note that the strain does not depend on the length of the wire, only the total extension does.
key_formulas: Series (end to end): same load, \( \Delta L_{total} = \Delta L_{1} + \Delta L_{2} \)
Parallel (side by side): same extension, \( F = F_{1} + F_{2} \) with \( F_{i} \propto \dfrac{Y_{i}A_{i}}{L_{i}} \)
topics.worked_example:
A steel wire (\( Y = 2\times10^{11} \) Pa, length 1 m, area \( 10^{-6} \) m\(^2\)) and a brass wire (\( Y = 10^{11} \) Pa, same dimensions) are joined end to end and loaded with 100 N.

Steel: \( \Delta L = \dfrac{100\times1}{10^{-6}\times2\times10^{11}} = 0.5 \) mm; brass: \( 1 \) mm.

Total extension \( = 1.5 \) mm. Side by side with equal extension instead, the loads would split 2 : 1 in favour of steel.
common_mistakes: Adding extensions for wires hung side by side, or splitting the load for wires joined end to end
Sharing the load equally between parallel wires of different stiffness
Using the radius ratio instead of the area (radius squared) ratio
Thinking that a longer wire has a larger strain; only the extension is larger

topics.name: Shear Modulus and Bulk Modulus (Compressibility)
topics.summary: Two further moduli describe deformations that are not a simple stretch. When a tangential force acts on a face of area \( A \) while the opposite face is held, the body changes shape without changing volume; the shear modulus (modulus of rigidity) is \( G = \dfrac{F/A}{\theta} \), where the shearing strain is the small tilt angle \( \theta \approx \dfrac{\Delta x}{L} \) in radians. When uniform pressure acts on all sides, the volume changes; the bulk modulus is \( B = -\dfrac{\Delta P}{\Delta V/V} \). The minus sign is there because an increase in pressure always decreases the volume, so that \( B \) itself is a positive number. Compressibility is the reciprocal, \( k = \dfrac{1}{B} \), with unit Pa\(^{-1}\): easy to compress means small \( B \) and large \( k \). Gases have tiny bulk moduli (about \( 10^{5} \) Pa), liquids and solids very large ones (\( 10^{9} \) to \( 10^{11} \) Pa). Liquids have a bulk modulus but no shear modulus because their layers slide freely. The fractional volume change under a pressure rise is \( \dfrac{\Delta P}{B} \), and the same fraction gives the increase in density.
key_formulas: Fractional volume decrease \( = \dfrac{\Delta P}{B} = k\,\Delta P \)
topics.worked_example:
A pressure increase of \( 2\times10^{6} \) Pa reduces the volume of a solid by one part in a thousand.

\( B = -\dfrac{2\times10^{6}}{-10^{-3}} = 2\times10^{9} \) Pa, positive.

Compressibility \( = \dfrac{1}{2\times10^{9}} = 5\times10^{-10} \) Pa\(^{-1}\).
common_mistakes: Applying Young's modulus to a tangential force, or the shear modulus to a stretch
Dropping the minus sign and reporting a negative bulk modulus
Using the displacement of the top face as the shear strain instead of dividing by the height
Confusing bulk modulus with compressibility, which is its reciprocal

topics.name: Elastic Potential Energy and Applications of Elastic Behaviour of Materials
topics.summary: Stretching a wire slowly does work against the internal restoring forces, and this work is stored as elastic potential energy in the changed interatomic separations. Because the restoring force grows linearly from zero to its final value \( F \), the work is the area of a triangle, \( U = \tfrac12 F\,\Delta L \), never the full product \( F\,\Delta L \). Dividing by the volume \( AL \) gives the energy density \( u = \tfrac12\,\sigma\,\varepsilon = \tfrac12 Y\varepsilon^{2} = \dfrac{\sigma^{2}}{2Y} \), with unit J/m\(^3\), the same as pascal; it equals the area under the stress-strain curve. Since a wire is a spring of constant \( k = \dfrac{YA}{L} \), the energy is also \( \tfrac12 k(\Delta L)^{2} \), so doubling the extension quadruples the energy. Applications follow from keeping stress below the elastic limit: crane ropes are made thick so that the stress stays safely below the yield stress; a beam sags by \( \delta = \dfrac{Wl^{3}}{4bd^{3}Y} \), so depth is far more effective than breadth and I-section girders give depth without weight; steel is preferred for springs because its large \( Y \) gives a large restoring force; and the maximum height of a mountain is set by the rock at its base reaching its elastic limit.
key_formulas: \( U = \tfrac12 F\,\Delta L = \tfrac12 k(\Delta L)^{2} = \dfrac{YA(\Delta L)^{2}}{2L} \)
Sag of a centrally loaded beam \( \delta = \dfrac{Wl^{3}}{4bd^{3}Y} \)
Minimum rope area \( A = \dfrac{F}{\sigma_{max}} \); mountain height \( h = \dfrac{\sigma_{limit}}{\rho g} \)
topics.worked_example:
A steel wire (\( Y = 2\times10^{11} \) Pa, length 1 m, area \( 10^{-6} \) m\(^2\)) is stretched by 1 mm.

Final force \( F = \dfrac{YA\,\Delta L}{L} = 200 \) N.

Energy stored \( U = \tfrac12\times200\times10^{-3} = 0.1 \) J, not 0.2 J.
common_mistakes: Using \( F\,\Delta L \) instead of \( \tfrac12 F\,\Delta L \), as if the full force acted throughout the stretch
Treating stress divided by strain as an energy density (that ratio is Young's modulus)
Computing the work for a change of extension from the change alone instead of from the difference of energies
Assuming sag varies inversely with the first power of depth rather than its cube

questions.topic: Stress, Strain, and Hooke's Law
questions.question: Stress in a deformed body is defined as
options: the restoring force developed per unit cross-sectional area of the body
the applied force per unit length of the body
the change in length divided by the original length
the product of the applied force and the area on which it acts
questions.explanation:
When a body is deformed, internal restoring forces appear that oppose the deformation.

Stress is the magnitude of this restoring force per unit area: \( \sigma = \dfrac{F}{A} \).

Its SI unit is N/m\(^2\), also called the pascal (Pa).
questions.hint: Think of stress as force spread over an area, not over a length.
distractor_logic: Divides by length instead of area; stress is a force per unit area
This ratio is strain, not stress
Stress is force divided by area, not multiplied by it

questions.topic: Stress, Strain, and Hooke's Law
questions.question: The SI unit of stress is
options: no unit, it is a pure number
questions.explanation:
Stress is force per unit area: \( \sigma = \dfrac{F}{A} \).

Unit of force is N and unit of area is m\(^2\), so stress has the unit N/m\(^2\), which is the pascal.
questions.hint: Stress and pressure share the same unit.
distractor_logic: N is the unit of force alone, before dividing by area
N m is the unit of work or torque, not of force per area
Strain is dimensionless, but stress carries the unit of pressure

questions.topic: Stress, Strain, and Hooke's Law
questions.question: Strain is best described as
options: the restoring force per unit area, measured in N/m\(^2\)
the change in length of the body, measured in metres
the ratio of change in dimension to the original dimension, and it is dimensionless
the applied force per unit area, measured in pascal
questions.explanation:
Strain measures the fractional deformation: for a wire, longitudinal strain \( \varepsilon = \dfrac{\Delta L}{L} \).

Both numerator and denominator are lengths, so strain has no unit.
questions.hint: Strain compares a change to the original size, so the units cancel.
distractor_logic: That is the definition of stress, not strain
Strain is a ratio, not the absolute change in length
Force per area is stress, and strain has no unit

questions.topic: Stress, Strain, and Hooke's Law
questions.question: According to Hooke's law, for small deformations
options: stress is proportional to the square of strain
stress is inversely proportional to strain
stress is proportional to strain for every value of the applied load
stress is directly proportional to strain, up to the proportional limit
questions.explanation:
Hooke's law is the empirical statement that, for small deformations, \( \sigma \propto \varepsilon \), i.e. \( \sigma = k\,\varepsilon \), where \( k \) is a modulus of elasticity.

It holds only in the initial linear region of the stress-strain curve, up to the proportional limit.
questions.hint: Hooke's law is a straight-line relationship, valid only for small deformations.
distractor_logic: The relation is linear, not quadratic
Larger strain needs larger stress, so the relation is direct, not inverse
Beyond the proportional limit the linear relation fails, so it is not valid for every load

questions.topic: Stress, Strain, and Hooke's Law
questions.question: A wire of length 2 m is stretched by 1 mm. The longitudinal strain produced is
questions.explanation:
Longitudinal strain \( \varepsilon = \dfrac{\Delta L}{L} \).

Convert to the same unit: \( \Delta L = 1 \) mm \( = 10^{-3} \) m and \( L = 2 \) m.

\( \varepsilon = \dfrac{10^{-3}}{2} = 5\times10^{-4} \), which has no unit.
questions.hint: Convert millimetres to metres first, then divide by the original length.
distractor_logic: Divides by 1 m instead of the actual original length of 2 m
Strain is a ratio of lengths and carries no unit
Inverts the ratio and uses the original length over the extension

questions.topic: Stress, Strain, and Hooke's Law
questions.question: A force of 100 N acts normally on a cross-section of area \( 2\times10^{-6} \) m\(^2\). The stress is
questions.explanation:
Stress \( \sigma = \dfrac{F}{A} \).

\( \sigma = \dfrac{100}{2\times10^{-6}} = 5\times10^{7} \) N/m\(^2\).
questions.hint: Dividing by a very small area gives a very large stress.
distractor_logic: Inverts the ratio and computes area divided by force
Multiplies force by area instead of dividing
Correct magnitude but stress is not measured in newton

questions.topic: Stress, Strain, and Hooke's Law
questions.question: In which situation is the stress a shearing (tangential) stress?
options: A wire hangs vertically from a rigid support with a load at its lower end
A solid ball is held deep inside water where the pressure is uniform all around
A book resting on a table is pushed horizontally along its top cover while the bottom cover stays fixed
A vertical rod is compressed along its length by a weight placed on top
questions.explanation:
Shearing stress arises when the force is applied tangentially (parallel) to a face, so that layers slide relative to each other and the shape changes without a change in volume.

Pushing the top cover sideways while the bottom stays fixed is exactly this case.
questions.hint: Look for a force applied parallel to a surface, not perpendicular to it.
distractor_logic: A hanging loaded wire experiences tensile (longitudinal) stress
Uniform pressure all around produces hydraulic (volume) stress
A weight on top produces compressive longitudinal stress

questions.topic: Stress, Strain, and Hooke's Law
questions.question: The constant of proportionality between stress and strain in Hooke's law is called
questions.explanation:
Hooke's law: \( \sigma = k\,\varepsilon \).

The constant \( k \) is called the modulus of elasticity; its value depends on the material and on the type of deformation (Young's modulus, shear modulus or bulk modulus).
questions.hint: The word modulus refers to the ratio of stress to strain.
distractor_logic: Strain is the effect, not the proportionality constant
Stress is the cause, not the proportionality constant
Compressibility is the reciprocal of one particular modulus, not the general constant

questions.topic: Stress-Strain Curve: Elastic Limit, Yield Point, and Fracture
questions.question: On the stress-strain curve of a metal wire, Hooke's law is obeyed
options: only up to the proportional limit
right up to the fracture point
questions.explanation:
Hooke's law requires stress to be directly proportional to strain, which shows as a straight line through the origin.

This straight portion ends at the proportional limit; beyond it the curve bends even though the material may still be elastic.
questions.hint: Look for the end of the straight-line part of the graph.
distractor_logic: Between the proportional limit and the yield point the curve is no longer straight
Far beyond the linear region the material deforms plastically, with no proportionality at all
Beyond the elastic limit the deformation is permanent and certainly not Hookean

questions.topic: Stress-Strain Curve: Elastic Limit, Yield Point, and Fracture
questions.question: The elastic limit of a material is
options: the stress at which the body breaks
the maximum stress up to which the body regains its original shape and size when the load is removed
the point where strain increases sharply with almost no increase in stress
the maximum stress the material can ever withstand
questions.explanation:
Up to the elastic limit the deformation is fully reversible: remove the load and the body returns exactly to its original dimensions.

Beyond it, some permanent (plastic) deformation remains.
questions.hint: Elastic means the body springs back completely.
distractor_logic: Breaking happens at the fracture point, which lies well beyond the elastic limit
That describes the yield point, which comes after the elastic limit
That is the ultimate tensile strength, a much larger stress

questions.topic: Stress-Strain Curve: Elastic Limit, Yield Point, and Fracture
questions.question: When a wire is loaded beyond its yield point and then unloaded, the deformation that remains is called
options: zero deformation, since the wire recovers fully
questions.explanation:
Beyond the yield point the material flows: the strain increases greatly and the atoms rearrange.

On unloading, the wire does not return to its original length; the remaining strain is plastic or permanent deformation.
questions.hint: Elastic recovers, plastic stays.
distractor_logic: Elastic deformation is the part that recovers, not the part that remains
Full recovery happens only if loading stayed within the elastic limit
Unloading does not reverse the shape beyond the original; it simply leaves a permanent set

questions.topic: Stress-Strain Curve: Elastic Limit, Yield Point, and Fracture
questions.question: The fracture point on a stress-strain curve is the point at which
options: stress stops being proportional to strain
strain begins to increase rapidly with little increase in stress
questions.explanation:
The fracture (breaking) point is the last point of the curve: here the material cannot sustain the load any further and it snaps.

It comes after the proportional limit, elastic limit and yield point, in that order.
questions.hint: Fracture is the final event on the curve.
distractor_logic: That is the proportional limit
That describes the yield point
That is the elastic limit

questions.topic: Stress-Strain Curve: Elastic Limit, Yield Point, and Fracture
questions.question: Moving along the stress-strain curve of a ductile metal from the origin, the correct order of the special points is
options: proportional limit, elastic limit, yield point, fracture point
elastic limit, proportional limit, yield point, fracture point
yield point, proportional limit, elastic limit, fracture point
proportional limit, yield point, elastic limit, fracture point
questions.explanation:
The straight line ends first at the proportional limit.

Slightly further, the elastic limit marks the end of full recovery.

Then the yield point, where large strain appears for little extra stress, and finally the fracture point where the wire breaks.
questions.hint: Straight line ends, recovery ends, flow begins, wire breaks.
distractor_logic: Swaps the first two: linearity ends before full elasticity ends
Places yielding first, but yielding happens only after elasticity is lost
Swaps the elastic limit and the yield point; the material is still elastic before it yields

questions.topic: Stress-Strain Curve: Elastic Limit, Yield Point, and Fracture
questions.question: A material that shows a large plastic region between its elastic limit and its fracture point is called
questions.explanation:
Ductile materials, such as copper and mild steel, can be stretched a great deal beyond the elastic limit before breaking.

This long plastic region is what allows them to be drawn into wires.
questions.hint: Ductile means drawable into wires.
distractor_logic: Brittle materials break soon after the elastic limit, with almost no plastic region
Elastomers show a very large elastic (not plastic) strain and do not obey Hooke's law
A perfectly elastic material would have no plastic region at all

questions.topic: Stress-Strain Curve: Elastic Limit, Yield Point, and Fracture
questions.question: Which statement about the stress-strain curve of rubber (an elastomer) is correct?
options: It obeys Hooke's law throughout its range
Rubber breaks after a very small strain
It is not a straight line, the strain is very large, and the rubber still returns to its original length
Rubber shows a large permanent deformation on unloading
questions.explanation:
Rubber can be stretched to several times its length and still snap back, so it is elastic.

However, its stress-strain curve is strongly curved with no proportional region, so Hooke's law does not apply.
questions.hint: Elastic does not mean Hookean.
distractor_logic: There is no linear region on the rubber curve, so Hooke's law is not obeyed
Rubber withstands very large strains before breaking
Rubber returns to its original length; it has practically no plastic deformation

questions.topic: Stress-Strain Curve: Elastic Limit, Yield Point, and Fracture
questions.question: The ultimate tensile strength of a material is
options: the stress at the proportional limit
the strain at the breaking point
the maximum stress the material can withstand before it starts to fail
questions.explanation:
The highest point on the stress-strain curve is the ultimate tensile strength.

Beyond it the wire begins to thin at some place (necking) and breaks at the fracture point, sometimes at a slightly lower stress.
questions.hint: Look for the peak of the curve.
distractor_logic: The proportional limit is a much smaller stress, near the start of the curve
Ultimate strength is a stress, not a strain
Young's modulus is the slope of the linear part, not the peak stress

questions.topic: Young's Modulus: Elongation, Compression, and Combined-Wire Problems
questions.question: A wire of length \( L \) and cross-sectional area \( A \) is stretched by \( \Delta L \) under a force \( F \). Young's modulus of the material is
questions.explanation:
Young's modulus is longitudinal stress divided by longitudinal strain.

\( Y = \dfrac{F/A}{\Delta L/L} = \dfrac{FL}{A\,\Delta L} \).
questions.hint: Stress over strain: put the extension in the denominator.
distractor_logic: Puts the extension in the numerator and the original length in the denominator, inverting the strain
Multiplies by the area instead of dividing; stress is force over area
This is the reciprocal of Young's modulus

questions.topic: Young's Modulus: Elongation, Compression, and Combined-Wire Problems
questions.question: The SI unit of Young's modulus is
questions.explanation:
\( Y = \dfrac{\text{stress}}{\text{strain}} \).

Strain has no unit, so Young's modulus has the unit of stress, N/m\(^2\) or pascal.
questions.hint: Same unit as stress, because strain is a pure number.
distractor_logic: Newton is the unit of force, not of force per area
Metre is a length; Young's modulus is a stress
Strain is unitless, but stress is not, so their ratio carries a unit

questions.topic: Young's Modulus: Elongation, Compression, and Combined-Wire Problems
questions.question: Steel has a much larger Young's modulus than rubber. This means that, for the same stress,
options: steel is stretched much more than rubber
steel is stretched much less than rubber
steel stretches permanently while rubber does not
questions.explanation:
Strain \( = \dfrac{\sigma}{Y} \). A larger \( Y \) means a smaller strain for the same stress.

So steel, with the larger \( Y \), is much harder to stretch, which is why it is called more elastic in physics.
questions.hint: Large modulus means large resistance to deformation.
distractor_logic: Reverses the relation; larger modulus means smaller strain
Different moduli produce different strains under the same stress
Young's modulus says nothing about permanence; it concerns the size of the elastic strain

questions.topic: Young's Modulus: Elongation, Compression, and Combined-Wire Problems
questions.question: A steel wire of length 2 m and cross-sectional area \( 10^{-6} \) m\(^2\) is stretched by a force of 200 N. Taking \( Y = 2\times10^{11} \) Pa for steel, the extension of the wire is
questions.explanation:
\( \Delta L = \dfrac{FL}{AY} \).

\( \Delta L = \dfrac{200\times2}{10^{-6}\times2\times10^{11}} = \dfrac{400}{2\times10^{5}} = 2\times10^{-3} \) m \( = 2 \) mm.
questions.hint: Rearrange the definition of Young's modulus to isolate the extension.
distractor_logic: Mistakes the value in metres, \( 2\times10^{-3} \), for 2 m
Drops a factor of ten in the power-of-ten arithmetic
Uses \( L^{2} \) or doubles the force in error

questions.topic: Young's Modulus: Elongation, Compression, and Combined-Wire Problems
questions.question: The value of Young's modulus of a wire depends on
options: the material of the wire only
the cross-sectional area of the wire
the load hanging from the wire
questions.explanation:
Young's modulus is a property of the material.

A long or short, thick or thin wire of the same steel has the same \( Y \); only the extension changes with the dimensions and the load.
questions.hint: A modulus is a material constant, like density.
distractor_logic: Length affects the extension, not the modulus
Area affects the extension, not the modulus
Load affects the extension, not the modulus

questions.topic: Young's Modulus: Elongation, Compression, and Combined-Wire Problems
questions.question: A wire of length \( L \), area \( A \) and Young's modulus \( Y \) carries a load \( F \). Its extension is
questions.explanation:
From \( Y = \dfrac{FL}{A\,\Delta L} \), rearranging gives \( \Delta L = \dfrac{FL}{AY} \).

Extension grows with force and length, and shrinks with area and modulus.
questions.hint: A longer, thinner, softer wire under a bigger load stretches more.
distractor_logic: Swaps area and length; a thicker wire should stretch less, not more
This is the inverse of the extension
This is the strain, not the extension; multiply by \( L \) to get the extension

questions.topic: Young's Modulus: Elongation, Compression, and Combined-Wire Problems
questions.question: Two wires of the same material and same cross-sectional area carry the same load. If the second wire is twice as long as the first, its extension is
options: four times that of the first
questions.explanation:
\( \Delta L = \dfrac{FL}{AY} \), so with \( F \), \( A \) and \( Y \) fixed, \( \Delta L \propto L \).

Doubling the length doubles the extension (the strain, however, is the same).
questions.hint: Same strain in a longer wire gives a bigger total stretch.
distractor_logic: Inverts the proportionality
Confuses extension with strain; the strain is the same, the extension is not
Uses a square law, but extension is directly proportional to length

questions.topic: Young's Modulus: Elongation, Compression, and Combined-Wire Problems
questions.question: Given Young's moduli: steel \( 2\times10^{11} \) Pa, copper \( 1.1\times10^{11} \) Pa, aluminium \( 7\times10^{10} \) Pa, rubber about \( 5\times10^{8} \) Pa. Which of these is the most elastic in the sense used in physics?
questions.explanation:
In physics, the more elastic material is the one that resists deformation more strongly, i.e. the one with the larger Young's modulus.

Steel has the largest \( Y \) here, so it is the most elastic.
questions.hint: More elastic means harder to deform, not easier to stretch.
distractor_logic: Rubber stretches easily, which means it has the smallest modulus, so it is the least elastic in this sense
Copper has a smaller modulus than steel
Aluminium has an even smaller modulus than copper

questions.topic: Shear Modulus and Bulk Modulus (Compressibility)
questions.question: The shear modulus (modulus of rigidity) of a material is defined as
options: tangential stress divided by shear strain
normal stress divided by longitudinal strain
pressure change divided by volume strain
shear strain divided by tangential stress
questions.explanation:
When a tangential force \( F \) acts on a face of area \( A \), the shape changes and the shear angle is \( \theta \).

Shear modulus \( G = \dfrac{F/A}{\theta} \), tangential stress over shearing strain.
questions.hint: Shear is about tangential force and change of shape.
distractor_logic: That is Young's modulus, which describes stretching along a length
That is the bulk modulus, which describes change of volume
Inverts the definition

questions.topic: Shear Modulus and Bulk Modulus (Compressibility)
questions.question: The bulk modulus \( B \) of a material is given by
questions.explanation:
Under a uniform pressure change \( \Delta P \), the volume changes by \( \Delta V \).

Bulk modulus \( = \dfrac{\text{hydraulic stress}}{\text{volume strain}} = -\dfrac{\Delta P}{\Delta V/V} \).

Because an increase in pressure decreases the volume, \( \Delta V \) is negative when \( \Delta P \) is positive; the minus sign makes \( B \) positive.
questions.hint: Pressure over fractional volume change, with a sign that keeps the modulus positive.

Displacement \( \Delta x = \theta L = 10^{-2}\times0.1 = 10^{-3} \) m \( = 1 \) mm.
questions.hint: Stress, then angle, then multiply the angle by the height.
distractor_logic: Mistakes the shear angle \( 10^{-2} \) for a displacement in metres
Off by a factor of ten in the area or the final multiplication
Reports the shear angle with the wrong unit instead of the displacement

questions.topic: Shear Modulus and Bulk Modulus (Compressibility)
questions.question: The volume of a solid is reduced by one part in a thousand when the pressure on it is increased by \( 2\times10^{6} \) Pa. Its bulk modulus is
questions.hint: One part in a thousand is a volume strain of \( 10^{-3} \).
distractor_logic: Multiplies by \( 10^{-3} \) instead of dividing
Drops the minus sign in the definition and leaves the modulus negative
Inverts the whole ratio and gets a compressibility-like number

questions.topic: Shear Modulus and Bulk Modulus (Compressibility)
questions.question: Given bulk moduli: steel \( 1.6\times10^{11} \) Pa, water \( 2.2\times10^{9} \) Pa, air (at ordinary conditions) about \( 10^{5} \) Pa. Which of these has the greatest compressibility?
options: all three have the same compressibility
questions.explanation:
Compressibility \( k = \dfrac{1}{B} \).

The smallest bulk modulus gives the largest compressibility, so air is by far the most compressible.
questions.hint: Compressibility is inversely related to bulk modulus.
distractor_logic: Steel has the largest bulk modulus and hence the smallest compressibility
Water is far less compressible than air
The compressibilities differ by many orders of magnitude

questions.topic: Shear Modulus and Bulk Modulus (Compressibility)
questions.question: A rectangular block is fixed at its base and a force is applied parallel to its top face, so that the block tilts slightly without changing its volume. The modulus that governs this deformation is
questions.explanation:
A force parallel to a face produces tangential (shearing) stress, changing the shape of the block but not its volume.

The ratio of tangential stress to the shear angle is the shear modulus \( G \).
questions.hint: Change of shape with no change of volume is shear.
distractor_logic: Young's modulus governs stretching or compression along a length
Bulk modulus governs a change of volume under uniform pressure
Compressibility is the reciprocal of the bulk modulus and also concerns volume

questions.topic: Shear Modulus and Bulk Modulus (Compressibility)
questions.question: A solid sphere is lowered deep into the ocean, where it is squeezed uniformly on all sides by the water pressure. The modulus that determines how much its volume decreases is
options: none, because a solid cannot change its volume
questions.explanation:
Uniform pressure from all sides produces hydraulic (volume) stress and a volume strain \( \dfrac{\Delta V}{V} \).

Their ratio is the bulk modulus \( B \).
questions.hint: Pressure from all sides changes volume, not length or shape.
distractor_logic: Young's modulus applies to a force along one direction, not to uniform pressure
Shear modulus applies to tangential forces that change shape
Solids do compress slightly under pressure; their bulk modulus is large but finite

questions.topic: Shear Modulus and Bulk Modulus (Compressibility)
questions.question: The bulk modulus of a liquid is \( 2\times10^{9} \) Pa. When the pressure on it is increased by \( 4\times10^{5} \) Pa, the fractional decrease in its volume is
questions.explanation:
\( \dfrac{\Delta V}{V} = -\dfrac{\Delta P}{B} \).

Fractional decrease \( = \dfrac{4\times10^{5}}{2\times10^{9}} = 2\times10^{-4} \), a pure number (0.02 %).
questions.hint: Divide the pressure change by the bulk modulus.
distractor_logic: Divides the bulk modulus by the pressure change
A fractional change has no unit
Multiplies pressure and modulus instead of dividing

questions.topic: Elastic Potential Energy and Applications of Elastic Behaviour of Materials
questions.question: A steel wire (\( Y = 2\times10^{11} \) Pa) of length 1 m and cross-sectional area \( 10^{-6} \) m\(^2\) is stretched by 1 mm. The elastic potential energy stored is
questions.explanation:
Force at full extension: \( F = \dfrac{YA\,\Delta L}{L} = \dfrac{2\times10^{11}\times10^{-6}\times10^{-3}}{1} = 200 \) N.

\( U = \tfrac12 F\,\Delta L = \tfrac12\times200\times10^{-3} = 0.1 \) J.
questions.hint: Find the final force from Young's modulus, then use half of force times extension.
distractor_logic: Omits the factor of one-half
Halves the force but forgets to multiply by the extension
Applies the factor of one-half twice

questions.topic: Elastic Potential Energy and Applications of Elastic Behaviour of Materials
questions.question: A wire is under a stress of \( 2\times10^{8} \) Pa and its strain is \( 10^{-3} \). The elastic energy stored per unit volume is
questions.explanation: \( u = \tfrac12\,\sigma\,\varepsilon = \tfrac12\times2\times10^{8}\times10^{-3} = 10^{5} \) J/m\(^3\).
questions.hint: Half of stress times strain.
distractor_logic: Omits the factor of one-half
Divides stress by strain, which gives Young's modulus, not an energy density
Correct number but energy per unit volume is not measured in joule

questions.topic: Elastic Potential Energy and Applications of Elastic Behaviour of Materials
questions.question: If the extension of a wire (within the elastic limit) is doubled, the elastic potential energy stored in it becomes
questions.explanation:
\( U = \tfrac12 k\,(\Delta L)^{2} \) with \( k = \dfrac{YA}{L} \).

Energy is proportional to the square of the extension, so doubling the extension makes the energy four times.
questions.hint: Both the force and the extension double.
distractor_logic: Doubles only the extension and forgets that the force doubles too
Energy depends on the extension
Uses a cube law; the dependence is quadratic

questions.topic: Elastic Potential Energy and Applications of Elastic Behaviour of Materials
questions.question: Two wires of the same material and same length carry the same load. Wire 1 has twice the cross-sectional area of wire 2. The ratio of the elastic energy stored in wire 1 to that in wire 2 is
questions.explanation:
Same load, so \( U = \tfrac12 F\,\Delta L \propto \Delta L \).

\( \Delta L = \dfrac{FL}{AY} \propto \dfrac{1}{A} \), so the thicker wire stretches half as much and stores half the energy: \( U_{1} : U_{2} = 1 : 2 \).
questions.hint: Same force, so compare the extensions.
distractor_logic: Inverts the ratio; the thicker wire stretches less and stores less energy
Squares the area ratio, but with a fixed load the energy varies inversely with area, not with its square
Different extensions under the same load mean different stored energies

questions.topic: Elastic Potential Energy and Applications of Elastic Behaviour of Materials
questions.question: Steel girders used in buildings and bridges are often given an I-shaped cross-section. The reason is that this shape
options: provides a large depth to resist bending while keeping the weight and cost of steel low
makes the girder heavier and therefore stronger
increases the Young's modulus of the steel
allows the girder to bend more easily
questions.explanation:
Bending resistance rises as the cube of the depth, so a deep beam is wanted.

An I-section keeps the two flanges far apart (large depth) but removes material from the middle where it contributes little, saving weight and cost while resisting bending.
questions.hint: Depth resists bending; the I shape gives depth without bulk.
distractor_logic: The point is to reduce weight, not increase it
Shape cannot change a material constant
A girder is meant to bend as little as possible

questions.topic: Elastic Potential Energy and Applications of Elastic Behaviour of Materials
questions.question: A wire of volume \( 2\times10^{-6} \) m\(^3\) is under a stress of \( 10^{8} \) Pa with a strain of \( 5\times10^{-4} \). The total elastic energy stored in the wire is
questions.explanation:
Energy density \( u = \tfrac12\,\sigma\,\varepsilon = \tfrac12\times10^{8}\times5\times10^{-4} = 2.5\times10^{4} \) J/m\(^3\).

Total energy \( U = u\times V = 2.5\times10^{4}\times2\times10^{-6} = 0.05 \) J.
questions.hint: Energy density times volume gives the total energy.
distractor_logic: Omits the factor of one-half
Reports the energy density as if it were the total energy
Correct number but the total energy is in joule, not joule per cubic metre

questions.topic: Elastic Potential Energy and Applications of Elastic Behaviour of Materials
questions.question: A steel rope is to lift a load of \( 10^{5} \) N. If the stress in the rope must not exceed \( 2\times10^{8} \) Pa, the minimum cross-sectional area of the rope is
questions.explanation:
Stress \( = \dfrac{F}{A}\le 2\times10^{8} \), so \( A \ge \dfrac{F}{\sigma_{max}} \).

\( A_{min} = \dfrac{10^{5}}{2\times10^{8}} = 5\times10^{-4} \) m\(^2\).
questions.hint: Area must be at least the load divided by the allowed stress.
distractor_logic: Area is measured in m\(^2\), not m
Divides the allowed stress by the load instead of the load by the stress
Power-of-ten slip in the division

questions.topic: Elastic Potential Energy and Applications of Elastic Behaviour of Materials
questions.question: The maximum height of a mountain is limited by the elastic limit of the rock at its base. If the rock yields at a stress of \( 3\times10^{8} \) Pa, its density is \( 3\times10^{3} \) kg/m\(^3\) and \( g = 10 \) m/s\(^2\), the maximum height is about
questions.explanation:
The stress at the base of a column of rock of height \( h \) is \( \rho g h \).

Setting \( \rho g h = 3\times10^{8} \): \( h = \dfrac{3\times10^{8}}{3\times10^{3}\times10} = 10^{4} \) m \( = 10 \) km.
questions.hint: Equate the pressure of the rock column to the yield stress.
distractor_logic: Power-of-ten slip: \( 10^{4} \) m is 10 km, not 10 m
Forgets to divide by \( g \)
Divides by an extra factor of a hundred

questions.topic: Stress, Strain, and Hooke's Law
questions.question: A wire of length \( L \), radius \( r \) and Young's modulus \( Y \) carries a load \( F \). It is replaced by a wire of the same material with length \( 2L \) and radius \( 2r \) carrying the same load. The longitudinal strain in the new wire, compared with the old, is
questions.explanation:
Strain \( \varepsilon = \dfrac{\sigma}{Y} = \dfrac{F}{AY} \), which does not depend on length.

Doubling the radius makes \( A = \pi r^{2} \) four times larger.

So the strain becomes \( \dfrac{F}{4AY} \), one-fourth of the original.
questions.hint: Strain depends on stress and Young's modulus only; length does not enter.
distractor_logic: Treats area as proportional to radius instead of its square
Ignores the change in cross-sectional area
Wrongly assumes strain grows with the doubled length; only the extension does

questions.topic: Stress, Strain, and Hooke's Law
questions.question: Stress has the same dimensions as
questions.explanation:
Stress \( = \dfrac{F}{A} \) has dimensions \( [ML^{-1}T^{-2}] \).

Energy per unit volume \( = \dfrac{[ML^{2}T^{-2}]}{[L^{3}]} = [ML^{-1}T^{-2}] \), the same.

This is why the elastic energy density \( \tfrac12\sigma\varepsilon \) has the unit of stress.
questions.hint: Write out the base dimensions of force over area and compare.
distractor_logic: Force per unit length is \( [MT^{-2}] \), the dimension of surface tension
Work has dimensions \( [ML^{2}T^{-2}] \)
Power per area is \( [MT^{-3}] \), which includes an extra inverse time

questions.topic: Stress, Strain, and Hooke's Law
questions.question: A wire of length 4 m and cross-sectional area 2 mm\(^2\) is stretched by 2 mm under a force of 400 N. The stress and strain are respectively
questions.explanation:
Area \( A = 2 \) mm\(^2\) \( = 2\times10^{-6} \) m\(^2\).

Stress \( \sigma = \dfrac{400}{2\times10^{-6}} = 2\times10^{8} \) Pa.

Strain \( \varepsilon = \dfrac{2\times10^{-3}}{4} = 5\times10^{-4} \), unitless.
distractor_logic: Attaches a unit to strain, which is a pure ratio
Uses the area in mm\(^2\) without converting to m\(^2\)
Divides 2 mm by 4 m without converting units, giving a strain that is a thousand times too large

questions.topic: Stress, Strain, and Hooke's Law
questions.question: A wire obeying Hooke's law develops a strain of 0.01 under a stress \( \sigma \). The stress required to produce a strain of 0.02 in the same wire (still within the proportional limit) is
questions.explanation:
Within the proportional limit, \( \sigma \propto \varepsilon \).

Doubling the strain from 0.01 to 0.02 therefore requires exactly double the stress, \( 2\sigma \).
questions.hint: Hooke's law is a direct, linear proportion.
distractor_logic: Inverts the proportion; more strain needs more stress
Uses a square law, but Hooke's law is linear
Assumes stress stays fixed while strain changes, which contradicts Hooke's law

questions.topic: Stress, Strain, and Hooke's Law
questions.question: A long uniform heavy wire of length \( L \) and density \( \rho \) hangs vertically from a rigid support, with no extra load. Which statement about the stress in the wire is correct?
options: The stress is maximum at the top and equals \( \rho g L \) there
The stress is maximum at the bottom and equals \( \rho g L \) there
The stress is the same at every cross-section of the wire
The stress is zero at the top support
questions.explanation:
A cross-section at distance \( x \) from the bottom must support the weight of the wire below it: \( W = \rho A x g \).

Stress at that section \( = \dfrac{\rho A x g}{A} = \rho g x \).

It is zero at the free bottom end and grows to \( \rho g L \) at the top, where the whole weight hangs.
questions.hint: Each section supports only the wire below it.
distractor_logic: The bottom end supports no wire below it, so the stress there is zero, not maximum
Uniform stress holds only for a light wire with a single end load; a heavy wire supports more of its own weight higher up
The top section supports the entire weight, so the stress there is largest

questions.topic: Stress, Strain, and Hooke's Law
questions.question: A wire is stretched so that its longitudinal strain is \( 2\times10^{-3} \) and its lateral (transverse) strain is \( -5\times10^{-4} \). The Poisson's ratio of the material is
questions.explanation:
Poisson's ratio \( \nu = -\dfrac{\text{lateral strain}}{\text{longitudinal strain}} \).

\( \nu = -\dfrac{-5\times10^{-4}}{2\times10^{-3}} = \dfrac{5\times10^{-4}}{2\times10^{-3}} = 0.25 \).

It is a ratio of two strains, so it is dimensionless and positive.
questions.hint: The negative sign in the definition cancels the negative lateral strain.
distractor_logic: Inverts the ratio, dividing longitudinal by lateral strain
Forgets the negative sign in the definition, leaving Poisson's ratio negative
A ratio of two strains has no unit

questions.topic: Stress-Strain Curve: Elastic Limit, Yield Point, and Fracture
questions.question: For a wire, the following stress-strain data are recorded: stress \( 100 \) MPa at strain \( 5\times10^{-4} \), stress \( 200 \) MPa at strain \( 1\times10^{-3} \), and stress \( 280 \) MPa at strain \( 1.5\times10^{-3} \). From this data, the proportional limit
options: lies at a strain of at least \( 1\times10^{-3} \) but below \( 1.5\times10^{-3} \)
cannot exist because Hooke's law is not obeyed by this wire
questions.explanation:
From the first two readings, \( \dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon} = \dfrac{100}{5\times10^{-4}} = \dfrac{200}{1\times10^{-3}} = 2\times10^{5} \) MPa, so the wire is linear up to at least strain \( 10^{-3} \).

At strain \( 1.5\times10^{-3} \) the linear prediction is \( 300 \) MPa, but only \( 280 \) MPa is observed.

So proportionality has failed somewhere between \( 10^{-3} \) and \( 1.5\times10^{-3} \).
questions.hint: Check whether stress divided by strain stays constant from one reading to the next.
distractor_logic: The first two readings already show perfect proportionality, so the limit is not below the first reading
The third reading falls short of the linear prediction, so proportionality has already failed before it
The first two points obey Hooke's law exactly

questions.topic: Stress-Strain Curve: Elastic Limit, Yield Point, and Fracture
questions.question: A wire is stretched to a total strain of \( 3\times10^{-3} \), which is beyond its elastic limit. When the load is removed, a permanent strain of \( 1\times10^{-3} \) remains. The strain recovered elastically on unloading is
questions.explanation:
Total strain under load = elastic (recoverable) strain + plastic (permanent) strain.

Elastic strain \( = 3\times10^{-3} - 1\times10^{-3} = 2\times10^{-3} \).
questions.hint: What springs back is the total minus what stays behind.
distractor_logic: Assumes the entire strain is recovered, ignoring the permanent set
Reports the permanent strain instead of the recovered strain
Adds the two strains instead of subtracting

questions.topic: Stress-Strain Curve: Elastic Limit, Yield Point, and Fracture
questions.question: Material A breaks at a strain of about 0.002, immediately after its linear region ends. Material B has a linear region, then a long nearly flat region, and breaks at a strain of about 0.2. Which identification is correct?
options: A is brittle and B is ductile
A is ductile and B is brittle
Both A and B are brittle
questions.explanation:
A fails almost at once after the elastic region, with negligible plastic strain: the signature of a brittle material.

B has a long plastic (flat) region and reaches a large strain before breaking: the signature of a ductile metal.
questions.hint: Compare the size of the plastic region before fracture.
distractor_logic: Swaps the two labels
B stretches a hundred times further than A before breaking, so it is not brittle
An elastomer has no linear region and no flat plastic region; B has both

questions.topic: Stress-Strain Curve: Elastic Limit, Yield Point, and Fracture
questions.question: For a ductile metal, the fracture point on the stress-strain curve is often at a slightly lower stress than the ultimate tensile strength. This is because
options: the material heals itself after reaching the maximum stress
after the ultimate strength the wire develops a neck, so it can carry less force before it breaks
stress can never decrease once a body is under load
Hooke's law forces the curve to turn downward
questions.explanation:
Beyond the ultimate tensile strength point, the wire begins to thin sharply at one place (necking).

The reduced cross-section there cannot support as much load, so the nominal stress falls until the wire finally breaks at the fracture point.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to the cross-section just before a metal wire snaps.
distractor_logic: Materials do not heal under increasing load
The stress in a wire can fall if the load it can bear falls
Hooke's law applies only to the initial linear region, far from the fracture point

questions.topic: Stress-Strain Curve: Elastic Limit, Yield Point, and Fracture
questions.question: The elastic limit of a steel wire corresponds to a stress of \( 2\times10^{8} \) Pa, and its Young's modulus is \( 2\times10^{11} \) Pa. Assuming the wire is linear up to the elastic limit, the maximum strain it can undergo and still recover fully is
questions.explanation:
Within the linear region \( \varepsilon = \dfrac{\sigma}{Y} \).

\( \varepsilon_{max} = \dfrac{2\times10^{8}}{2\times10^{11}} = 10^{-3} \), a pure number.
questions.hint: Divide the limiting stress by Young's modulus.
distractor_logic: Divides Young's modulus by stress instead of stress by Young's modulus
Strain has no unit
Multiplies stress and modulus instead of dividing

questions.topic: Stress-Strain Curve: Elastic Limit, Yield Point, and Fracture
questions.question: A steel wire of length 2 m has Young's modulus \( 2\times10^{11} \) Pa and its yield point corresponds to a stress of \( 4\times10^{8} \) Pa. Treating the wire as linear up to the yield point, the maximum elongation it can be given before it begins to yield is
questions.explanation:
Strain at yield \( = \dfrac{\sigma}{Y} = \dfrac{4\times10^{8}}{2\times10^{11}} = 2\times10^{-3} \).

Elongation \( \Delta L = \varepsilon L = 2\times10^{-3}\times2 = 4\times10^{-3} \) m \( = 4 \) mm.
questions.hint: Find the strain first, then multiply by the original length.
distractor_logic: Forgets to multiply the strain by the 2 m length
Doubles the extension by mixing up strain and elongation
Reports the answer in metres while the value is in millimetres

questions.topic: Young's Modulus: Elongation, Compression, and Combined-Wire Problems
questions.question: A steel wire (\( Y = 2\times10^{11} \) Pa) and a brass wire (\( Y = 1\times10^{11} \) Pa) of equal length and equal cross-sectional area hang side by side from a rigid support and together carry a load of 300 N through a rigid bar, so that both extend by the same amount. The loads carried by the steel and brass wires are respectively
questions.explanation:
Side by side (parallel): equal extension, and the loads add up to 300 N.

\( F = \dfrac{YA}{L}\Delta L \), so with the same \( A \), \( L \) and \( \Delta L \), \( F \propto Y \).

\( F_{steel} : F_{brass} = 2 : 1 \), giving 200 N and 100 N.
questions.hint: Equal stretch means the stiffer wire takes the larger share of the load.
distractor_logic: Splits the load equally, ignoring the different Young's moduli
Gives the larger load to the softer wire, reversing the ratio
Ignores the brass wire entirely; both wires stretch and both carry load

questions.topic: Young's Modulus: Elongation, Compression, and Combined-Wire Problems
questions.question: Wire 1 (length 1 m, area \( 10^{-6} \) m\(^2\), \( Y = 2\times10^{11} \) Pa) and wire 2 (length 2 m, area \( 2\times10^{-6} \) m\(^2\), \( Y = 1\times10^{11} \) Pa) are joined end to end, and a load of 200 N hangs from the bottom. The total extension is
questions.explanation:
Series: same load in each wire; extensions add.

Wire 1: \( \dfrac{200\times1}{10^{-6}\times2\times10^{11}} = 10^{-3} \) m \( = 1 \) mm.

Wire 2: \( \dfrac{200\times2}{2\times10^{-6}\times10^{11}} = 2\times10^{-3} \) m \( = 2 \) mm.

Total \( = 3 \) mm.
questions.hint: Compute each extension separately with the full load, then add.
distractor_logic: Reports the extension of wire 1 alone
Reports the extension of wire 2 alone
Averages the two extensions instead of adding them

questions.topic: Young's Modulus: Elongation, Compression, and Combined-Wire Problems
questions.question: A wire of length \( L \) extends by \( \Delta L \) under a load \( F \). The wire is cut into two equal halves and the same load is hung from one half. The extension of the half-wire is
questions.explanation:
\( \Delta L = \dfrac{FL}{AY} \). Cutting the wire changes only \( L \) to \( \dfrac{L}{2} \).

The extension becomes \( \dfrac{F(L/2)}{AY} = \dfrac{\Delta L}{2} \).

The stress and strain are unchanged; only the shorter length gives a smaller total stretch.
questions.hint: Half the length at the same strain gives half the extension.
distractor_logic: Confuses strain (unchanged) with extension (halved)
Inverts the effect of the shorter length
Applies a square-law reduction that has no basis here

questions.topic: Young's Modulus: Elongation, Compression, and Combined-Wire Problems
questions.question: A steel wire (\( Y = 2\times10^{11} \) Pa) and a copper wire (\( Y = 1.1\times10^{11} \) Pa) of equal length and equal cross-sectional area are joined end to end and loaded. The ratio of the strain in steel to the strain in copper is
options: the strains cannot be compared because the stresses are different
questions.explanation:
In series the same force passes through both wires, and the areas are equal, so the stress is the same in both.

\( \varepsilon = \dfrac{\sigma}{Y} \), so \( \dfrac{\varepsilon_{steel}}{\varepsilon_{copper}} = \dfrac{Y_{copper}}{Y_{steel}} = \dfrac{1.1}{2} = \dfrac{11}{20} \).
questions.hint: Equal stress in series; the stiffer wire has the smaller strain.
distractor_logic: Inverts the ratio; the wire with the larger modulus strains less
Equal stress does not imply equal strain when the moduli differ
The stresses are equal here, so the strains can be compared directly

questions.topic: Young's Modulus: Elongation, Compression, and Combined-Wire Problems
questions.question: Two wires of the same material and equal length, with cross-sectional areas \( A \) and \( 2A \), hang side by side and jointly support a load \( F \) so that both stretch equally. The load carried by the thicker wire is
questions.explanation:
Parallel: equal extension, loads add.

\( F_{i} = \dfrac{YA_{i}}{L}\Delta L \), so the loads are in the ratio of the areas, \( 1 : 2 \).

Thicker wire carries \( \dfrac{2}{3}F \), thinner wire carries \( \dfrac{1}{3}F \).
questions.hint: Equal stretch, so load shares follow the areas.
distractor_logic: Splits the load equally, ignoring the different areas
Gives the thicker wire the smaller share
Ignores the thinner wire; both wires share the load

questions.topic: Young's Modulus: Elongation, Compression, and Combined-Wire Problems
questions.question: A wire is stretched so that its length increases by 0.1 %. If the Poisson's ratio of the material is 0.3, the diameter of the wire
questions.explanation:
Longitudinal strain \( \varepsilon = 10^{-3} \).

Lateral strain \( = -\nu\varepsilon = -0.3\times10^{-3} = -3\times10^{-4} \).

A lateral strain of \( -3\times10^{-4} \) means the diameter decreases by 0.03 %.
questions.hint: Lateral strain is Poisson's ratio times longitudinal strain, with opposite sign.
distractor_logic: Gets the sign wrong; a stretched wire becomes thinner, not thicker
Forgets to multiply by Poisson's ratio
A non-zero Poisson's ratio always produces a lateral change

questions.topic: Shear Modulus and Bulk Modulus (Compressibility)
questions.question: A liquid has compressibility \( 5\times10^{-10} \) Pa\(^{-1}\). When the pressure on it is increased by \( 10^{7} \) Pa, its volume decreases by
questions.explanation:
Fractional decrease \( = \dfrac{\Delta P}{B} = k\,\Delta P \).

\( = 5\times10^{-10}\times10^{7} = 5\times10^{-3} = 0.5\% \).
questions.hint: Compressibility times pressure change gives the fractional volume change directly.
distractor_logic: Divides the bulk modulus by the pressure change instead of the pressure change by the bulk modulus
A fractional change has no unit; the absolute change would need the original volume
Divides the pressure change by the compressibility instead of multiplying

questions.topic: Shear Modulus and Bulk Modulus (Compressibility)
questions.question: A rubber ball of volume \( 10^{-3} \) m\(^3\) is taken to a depth where the pressure is \( 10^{6} \) Pa more than at the surface. If the bulk modulus of rubber is \( 10^{9} \) Pa, the decrease in the volume of the ball is
questions.hint: Find the fractional change, then multiply by the original volume.
distractor_logic: Reports the fractional change as if it were the absolute volume change
Multiplies by an extra factor of \( 10^{-3} \)
Divides the modulus by the pressure and forgets the original volume

questions.topic: Shear Modulus and Bulk Modulus (Compressibility)
questions.question: A tangential force of \( 2\times10^{4} \) N is applied to the top face of a cube of side 0.2 m, whose bottom face is fixed. The top face moves by 0.2 mm. The shear modulus of the material is
questions.explanation:
Face area \( A = 0.2\times0.2 = 0.04 \) m\(^2\); tangential stress \( = \dfrac{2\times10^{4}}{0.04} = 5\times10^{5} \) Pa.

Shear angle \( \theta = \dfrac{\Delta x}{L} = \dfrac{2\times10^{-4}}{0.2} = 10^{-3} \) rad.

\( G = \dfrac{5\times10^{5}}{10^{-3}} = 5\times10^{8} \) Pa.
questions.hint: Shear strain is the displacement divided by the height, not the displacement itself.
distractor_logic: Divides the stress by the displacement in metres instead of by the shear angle
Reports the tangential stress without dividing by the shear strain
A modulus is never negative; shear modulus has no sign convention issue

questions.topic: Shear Modulus and Bulk Modulus (Compressibility)
questions.question: The bulk modulus of water is \( 2\times10^{9} \) Pa. At a depth in the ocean where the pressure is \( 2\times10^{7} \) Pa greater than at the surface, the density of water is greater than at the surface by about
options: 0 %, since density does not change with pressure
questions.explanation:
Fractional decrease in volume \( = \dfrac{\Delta P}{B} = \dfrac{2\times10^{7}}{2\times10^{9}} = 10^{-2} \).

Mass is fixed, so a 1 % decrease in volume means about a 1 % increase in density.
questions.hint: Same mass in a slightly smaller volume means a slightly larger density.
distractor_logic: Off by a factor of ten in the division
Off by a factor of ten the other way

questions.explanation:

questions.question: A wire of length \( L \) stores energy \( U \) when stretched by \( x \). The wire is cut into two equal halves and one half is stretched by the same \( x \). The energy stored in the half-wire is
questions.explanation:

Volume: \( \Delta P = B\times\dfrac{|\Delta V|}{V} = 1.6\times10^{11}\times10^{-3} = 1.6\times10^{8} \) Pa, a positive pressure increase.
questions.hint: Each strain type pairs with its own modulus.

questions.topic: Stress-Strain Curve: Elastic Limit, Yield Point, and Fracture
questions.question: A wire is stretched beyond its elastic limit and then unloaded. Compared with the work done in stretching it, the elastic energy recovered on unloading is
options: less, because part of the work went into permanent deformation and appears mainly as heat
exactly equal, because energy is always conserved as elastic energy
greater, because the wire releases extra energy on unloading
zero, because no work is done when a wire yields
questions.explanation:
Within the elastic limit the area under the stress-strain curve on loading and unloading is the same, so all the work is recovered.

Beyond the elastic limit the unloading curve does not return to the origin; the area enclosed between the two paths is energy that is not recovered as elastic energy but is dissipated, largely as heat, in producing the permanent deformation.
questions.hint: What happens to the work that produced the permanent set?
distractor_logic: Total energy is conserved, but not all of it stays as recoverable elastic energy
A wire cannot return more energy than was put in
Stretching a yielding wire still requires a force through a distance, so work is done

questions.topic: Young's Modulus: Elongation, Compression, and Combined-Wire Problems
questions.question: A steel wire (\( Y = 2\times10^{11} \) Pa, length 2 m) and a copper wire (\( Y = 1.1\times10^{11} \) Pa, length 1.1 m), each of cross-sectional area \( 10^{-6} \) m\(^2\), are joined end to end and a load of 100 N hangs from the free end. The stress in each wire and the total extension are
options: stress \( 10^{8} \) Pa in steel and \( 5\times10^{7} \) Pa in copper; total extension 1.5 mm
stress \( 10^{8} \) Pa in both; total extension 2 mm
stress \( 10^{8} \) Pa in both; total extension 1 mm
stress \( 10^{8} \) Pa in both; total extension 3.1 mm
questions.explanation:
Series: the same 100 N passes through both wires and the areas are equal, so the stress is \( \dfrac{100}{10^{-6}} = 10^{8} \) Pa in each.

Steel: \( \Delta L = \dfrac{100\times2}{10^{-6}\times2\times10^{11}} = 10^{-3} \) m \( = 1 \) mm.

Copper: \( \Delta L = \dfrac{100\times1.1}{10^{-6}\times1.1\times10^{11}} = 10^{-3} \) m \( = 1 \) mm.

Total \( = 2 \) mm.
questions.hint: Same load through both wires means same stress; extensions add.
distractor_logic: Splits the load between the wires as if they were in parallel
Counts only one of the two extensions
Adds the lengths of the wires instead of their extensions

questions.topic: Young's Modulus: Elongation, Compression, and Combined-Wire Problems
questions.question: Steel is preferred over copper for making springs. The reason is that
options: steel has a smaller Young's modulus, so it stretches more easily
copper cannot be deformed elastically at all
steel has a larger Young's modulus, so for the same deformation it exerts a larger restoring force and stores more energy
steel obeys Hooke's law but copper does not
questions.explanation:
A spring should produce a large restoring force and store much energy for a small deformation.

\( F = \dfrac{YA}{L}\Delta L \) and \( U = \dfrac{YA(\Delta L)^{2}}{2L} \); both are larger for the larger \( Y \) of steel (\( 2\times10^{11} \) Pa versus \( 1.1\times10^{11} \) Pa for copper).
questions.hint: A good spring is stiff and returns a lot of energy.
distractor_logic: Steel has the larger Young's modulus, and easy stretching is not what a spring needs
Copper is elastic within its own limit, just with a smaller modulus
Both metals obey Hooke's law for small strains

questions.topic: Stress, Strain, and Hooke's Law
questions.question: A wire is loaded in steps: 20 N produces an extension of 0.5 mm, 40 N produces 1.0 mm, and 60 N produces 1.8 mm. Which conclusion is correct?
options: The wire obeys Hooke's law throughout, since the extension increases with the load
The wire obeys Hooke's law up to at least 40 N, and its proportional limit lies between 40 N and 60 N
The wire does not obey Hooke's law even at 20 N
The wire has fractured at 60 N
questions.explanation:
From 20 N to 40 N the extension doubles with the load: \( \dfrac{F}{\Delta L} = 40 \) N/mm in both cases, so Hooke's law holds.

At 60 N Hooke's law predicts 1.5 mm, but 1.8 mm is observed, so proportionality has failed somewhere between 40 N and 60 N.
questions.hint: Check whether load divided by extension stays constant between readings.
distractor_logic: Increasing is not enough; the increase must be in proportion
The first two readings are in exact proportion
An extension of 1.8 mm is far from the strain needed to break a metal wire; the wire has merely left the linear region

questions.topic: Shear Modulus and Bulk Modulus (Compressibility)
questions.question: A submarine hull and a deep-sea instrument casing must both withstand very high pressure without their internal volume shrinking appreciably. The material property that matters most for this is
options: a small bulk modulus, i.e. a large compressibility
a large bulk modulus, i.e. a small compressibility
questions.explanation:
Uniform water pressure from all sides produces volume strain \( \dfrac{\Delta V}{V} = -\dfrac{\Delta P}{B} \).

To keep this change small for a large \( \Delta P \), the material must have a large bulk modulus, i.e. it must be hard to compress.
questions.hint: Resisting a change of volume under pressure is exactly what the bulk modulus measures.
distractor_logic: A large compressibility means the volume shrinks easily under pressure, the opposite of what is wanted
Young's modulus concerns stretching along one direction, not uniform compression, and a small value would be a disadvantage anyway
Shear strain is a deformation, not a material property, and a large one would be undesirable

questions.question: A rod of length \( L \), cross-sectional area \( A \) and Young's modulus \( Y \) is compressed along its length by a force \( F \). Its compressive strain is

Compressive stress \( = \dfrac{F}{A} \).

Strain \( = \dfrac{\text{stress}}{Y} = \dfrac{F}{AY} \), a dimensionless number; the decrease in length would be \( \dfrac{FL}{AY} \).
questions.hint: Strain is stress over Young's modulus and does not involve the length.

questions.topic: Stress-Strain Curve: Elastic Limit, Yield Point, and Fracture
questions.question: On a stress-strain curve, P is the proportional limit and E is the elastic limit, with E slightly beyond P. A wire is loaded to a point between P and E and then unloaded. Which statement is correct?
options: The wire retains a permanent strain, because Hooke's law was violated
The wire returns fully to its original length, but between P and E its stress was no longer proportional to its strain
The wire returns fully and Hooke's law held throughout, because P and E are the same point
questions.explanation:
Up to E the deformation is completely elastic, so unloading restores the original length.

But Hooke's law (linearity) holds only up to P; between P and E the graph curves, so stress and strain are no longer proportional even though recovery is still complete.
questions.hint: Linearity and full recovery end at two different points.
distractor_logic: Loss of proportionality does not cause permanent strain; only crossing the elastic limit does
P and E are distinct points; the elastic limit lies slightly beyond the proportional limit
Fracture occurs far beyond the elastic limit

questions.topic: Shear Modulus and Bulk Modulus (Compressibility)
questions.question: A cube is subjected to a uniform pressure of \( 10^{6} \) Pa from all sides, and a rod of the same material is subjected to a tensile stress of \( 10^{6} \) Pa along its length. For this material \( B = 10^{9} \) Pa and \( Y = 10^{11} \) Pa. The magnitudes of the volume strain of the cube and the longitudinal strain of the rod are
options: both \( 10^{-5} \), since the stress is the same
\( -10^{-3} \) and \( 10^{-5} \), with the bulk modulus taken as negative
questions.explanation:
Cube: uniform pressure, so use the bulk modulus: \( \dfrac{|\Delta V|}{V} = \dfrac{\Delta P}{B} = \dfrac{10^{6}}{10^{9}} = 10^{-3} \).

Rod: stress along one direction, so use Young's modulus: \( \varepsilon = \dfrac{\sigma}{Y} = \dfrac{10^{6}}{10^{11}} = 10^{-5} \).
questions.hint: Uniform pressure pairs with \( B \); a stretch along a length pairs with \( Y \).
distractor_logic: Swaps the two moduli between the two deformations
Uses Young's modulus for both, although uniform pressure produces a volume strain governed by \( B \)
The bulk modulus is positive; the minus sign in its definition only reflects that volume falls as pressure rises

questions.question: For a wire, the area under the stress-strain curve from the origin up to any point in the elastic region represents
options: the total elastic energy stored in the wire
the force applied to the wire
the elastic energy stored per unit volume of the wire
questions.explanation:
The area under a stress-strain graph has the dimensions of stress times strain, i.e. energy per unit volume.

In the linear region this area is a triangle, \( \tfrac12\,\sigma\,\varepsilon \), which is exactly the elastic energy density; multiplying by the volume gives the total energy.
questions.hint: Check the dimensions of stress times strain.
distractor_logic: The graph uses stress and strain, not force and extension, so the area is per unit volume
Young's modulus is the slope of the linear part, not the area under it
Force is not represented by an area on this graph

questions.topic: Stress, Strain, and Hooke's Law
questions.question: A force \( F \) is applied to a face of area \( A \) of a block, first perpendicular to the face and then parallel to it. In the two cases
options: the stress has the same magnitude \( \dfrac{F}{A} \) but is longitudinal in the first case and tangential in the second, so different moduli apply
the stress is \( \dfrac{F}{A} \) in the first case and zero in the second, since a parallel force produces no stress
the stress and the strain are identical in both cases
Young's modulus applies in both cases because the force and area are the same
questions.explanation:
Stress magnitude is \( \dfrac{F}{A} \) in both cases.

A perpendicular force produces longitudinal stress and strain, governed by Young's modulus \( Y \).

A parallel force produces tangential stress and shear strain, governed by the shear modulus \( G \). Same numbers, different physics.
questions.hint: Direction of the force relative to the face decides the type of stress.
distractor_logic: A tangential force produces a shearing stress, which is not zero
The moduli differ, so the strains differ even though the stresses are equal in magnitude
Young's modulus applies only to normal (perpendicular) stress

questions.topic: Young's Modulus: Elongation, Compression, and Combined-Wire Problems
questions.question: A wire of length \( L \) needs a force \( F \) to stretch it by \( x \) and stores energy \( U \) in doing so. The wire is cut in half. To stretch one half by the same \( x \), the force needed and the energy stored are
questions.explanation:
Spring constant \( k = \dfrac{YA}{L} \) doubles when \( L \) is halved.

Force \( = kx \) doubles to \( 2F \).

Energy \( = \tfrac12 k x^{2} \) doubles to \( 2U \), since \( x \) is unchanged.
questions.hint: A shorter wire is a stiffer spring.
distractor_logic: Ignores the change in stiffness caused by cutting the wire
Reverses the effect; a shorter wire is stiffer, not softer
Doubles the force but wrongly squares the energy factor; with fixed extension the energy scales with the spring constant

questions.topic: Stress-Strain Curve: Elastic Limit, Yield Point, and Fracture
questions.question: A wire of length 1.5 m stays elastic up to a strain of \( 2\times10^{-3} \). It is stretched by 4 mm and then released. Which statement is correct?
options: The elastic limit corresponds to a 3 mm extension, but the wire still returns exactly to 1.5 m
The elastic limit corresponds to a 6 mm extension, so the wire returns exactly to 1.5 m
The wire breaks, because 4 mm exceeds the elastic limit
The elastic limit corresponds to a 3 mm extension, so the 4 mm stretch leaves a permanent extension in the wire
questions.explanation:
Maximum elastic extension \( = \varepsilon L = 2\times10^{-3}\times1.5 = 3\times10^{-3} \) m \( = 3 \) mm.

A 4 mm stretch exceeds this, so part of the deformation is plastic and a permanent extension remains after release.

Exceeding the elastic limit does not by itself cause fracture.
questions.hint: Convert the limiting strain into an extension and compare.
distractor_logic: Full recovery is impossible once the elastic limit has been exceeded
Multiplies the strain by 3 m instead of 1.5 m
Fracture requires a much larger strain than the elastic limit

questions.topic: Shear Modulus and Bulk Modulus (Compressibility)
questions.question: The bulk modulus of air at ordinary conditions is about \( 10^{5} \) Pa and that of water is about \( 2\times10^{9} \) Pa. The ratio of the compressibility of air to that of water is
options: 1, since compressibility does not depend on the material
questions.explanation:
Compressibility \( k = \dfrac{1}{B} \).

\( \dfrac{k_{air}}{k_{water}} = \dfrac{B_{water}}{B_{air}} = \dfrac{2\times10^{9}}{10^{5}} = 2\times10^{4} \).

Air is twenty thousand times more compressible than water.
questions.hint: Ratio of compressibilities is the inverse ratio of bulk moduli.
distractor_logic: Uses the ratio of bulk moduli in the same order, instead of inverting it
Multiplies the two bulk moduli instead of dividing
Compressibility is a material property and varies enormously between air and water

\( U = \tfrac12 F\,\Delta L = \tfrac12\times400\times10^{-3} = 0.2 \) J.
